docs.text: UltraGPS Ground Station ¶ Ground control program for the St. Mary's University UltraGPS positioning system, developed as a result of graduate research. UltraGpsXY is designed to run on the ground-station host, which is the computer that is connected to the base-station Arduino + UltraGPS shield combo through USB. It maintains a serial link to the base-station and allows commands to be sent to the base-station from the network through a TCP command socket and a UDP data stream. This allows other computers, from within the same network, to communicate to the base-station without having to be physically connected to the base-station. This program must be running in order for the UltraGPSControl program to properly. Documentation ¶ Architecture — how the program is structured and how data flows between the Arduino, the modules, and network clients. Installation — building from source or installing the Debian package. Usage — running the program and its command-line options. At a glance ¶ Binary UltraGpsXY Language C++17 (CMake) Serial default /dev/ttyACM0 @ 38400 bps Default TCP command port 9000 Default UDP stream port 9001 Platform Linux (packaged for Ubuntu/Debian, amd64)

docs.text: Architecture ¶ UltraGpsXY is a single C++17 executable built with CMake. It is organised around a main.cpp control loop and four modules, plus third-party libraries that are compiled in statically. Components ¶ Component Location Responsibility Control loop main.cpp Argument parsing, module setup, banner, main event loop Comms module CommsModule/ Command validation and framing over the serial link; the command reference printed by help ( commandHelp.cpp ) Serial module SerialModule/ Low-level POSIX serial (termios) I/O to the Arduino, including switching the baud rate of the open port in place Server module ServerModule/ TCP command socket + UDP continuous data stream, TCP client limit, client list TUI module TuiModule/ Optional notcurses terminal UI ( --tui ): its own render/input thread, shared TuiState , and a ControlQueue of requests that the control loop executes Third-party libraries ¶ These are vendored as git submodules and statically linked , so the shipped binary has no third-party runtime dependencies: spdlog — logging. argparse — command-line parsing. The tomlplusplus submodule is still checked out but no longer used: the build does not include it. notcurses (core library only) — terminal UI. A submodule pinned to v3.0.17. CMake copies it into the build directory, applies notcurses-tmux-patch-cmake/ for the tmux variant ( -DULTRAGPS_TUI_TERMINAL=tmux ), and links it statically. Data flow ¶ Base-station Arduino │ (USB serial, e.g. /dev/ttyACM0 @ 38400) ▼ ┌──────────────┐ ┌──────────────┐ │ SerialModule │◄──────►│ CommsModule │ └──────────────┘ └──────┬───────┘ │ ┌───────▼────────┐ │ main() loop │ └───────┬────────┘ │ ┌───────▼────────┐ │ ServerModule │ └───────┬────────┘ TCP commands (9000) │ UDP stream (9001) ▼ Network clients Control loop ¶ The loop in main() runs continuously and, on each pass: Runs TUI requests from the control queue (empty when headless). Finishes a boot wait : once the base-station has booted after the port was opened or after B / M rebooted it at another baud rate, it switches the host side to that rate in place (no reopen, so no second DTR reset) and re-queries the board's settings. Receives TCP commands from network clients via the Server module. help / ? is answered here with the command reference, to the asking client only, and never forwarded. Validates each command through the Comms module, discarding anything invalid, and drops commands while the base-station is booting. Dispatches by command type: Normal commands are sent to the Arduino and the response is returned to the TCP clients. Continuous commands switch the system into streaming mode. Streams data : while in continuous mode, serial data from the Arduino is pushed out to clients over UDP. Logging ¶ Logging uses spdlog . The SPDLOG_* macros are gated at compile time by SPDLOG_ACTIVE_LEVEL : Default build — the macros are compiled out entirely. Direct calls such as spdlog::info() (banner, module-init messages) are always present, regardless of compilation debug level. -DVERBOSE_LOGGING=ON — all SPDLOG_* macros are active at DEBUG level and the build switches to a debug configuration. See Installation and Usage . Terminal UI threading ¶ The TUI thread never touches the serial port or Comms : Serial taps. Serial calls an RX and a TX callback for every complete line. These callbacks feed the "serial link" log, the tick history and the jitter windows (the tick lines of the last 10 s) in TuiState . Serial::getReceived() only keeps the latest line, so the taps are the only reliable way to see every line. Help. help / ? typed in the TUI never reaches the control loop: the TUI thread writes the command reference into the TuiState log itself. Control queue. Settings changes and commands typed in the TUI become a ControlRequest . The control loop drains the queue once per iteration and runs each request on its own thread, so baud/port reopens never race checkResponse() . Logging. While the TUI is active, spdlog's default logger is replaced by a callback sink (shown in the log pane) and a file sink ( ~/.local/state/ultragps/ultragpsxy.log ). Nothing writes to the terminal.

docs.text: Developer's Guide ¶ A self-contained reference for developers who fork the repository and need to work with the project's tooling — building, packaging, previewing the documentation, and cutting releases. Everything needed is on this page. Overview ¶ UltraGpsXY is a single C++17 executable that runs on the ground-station host and bridges the positioning hardware to the network: Maintains a serial link to the base-station Arduino (default /dev/ttyACM0 @ 38400 bps) via the Comms/Serial modules. Runs a TCP command server (default port 9000 ): network clients send commands, which are validated and forwarded to the Arduino, and the response is returned to the client. Runs a UDP data stream (default port 9001 ): while in continuous mode, live position data from the Arduino is streamed out to clients. The third-party libraries ( spdlog , argparse ) are included as git submodules and statically linked, so the installed binary has no third-party runtime dependencies. (The tomlplusplus submodule is still checked out, but the build no longer uses it.) Requirements ¶ A C++17 compiler (GCC or Clang) and CMake ≥ 3.15 git (the third-party libraries are git submodules) dpkg / cpack — only needed to build the .deb package Python 3 with pip — only needed to build/preview the documentation TUI build dependencies: libunistring-dev libncurses-dev zlib1g-dev ( sudo apt install ... ). notcurses itself comes from the notcurses submodule, so no network access is needed at build time. Clone with submodules: git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/Imperious22M/UltraGPS-Ground.git cd UltraGPS-Ground # If you already cloned without --recurse-submodules: git submodule update --init --recursive Installing a prebuilt release ¶ You don't need to build anything to run the program — each release ships a prebuilt Debian package. Download the latest .deb from the Releases page and install it: sudo dpkg -i ultragps-xy_*_amd64.deb # plain terminal sudo dpkg -i ultragps-xy-tmux_*_amd64.deb # or: TUI inside tmux This installs UltraGpsXY to /usr/bin (on your PATH ) and pulls in its runtime dependencies automatically. Using the build script ¶ build.sh is the single entry point for building, packaging, cleaning, and previewing the docs. Run it from the repository root: ./build.sh <command> [options] Commands ¶ Command What it does build Compile the UltraGpsXY binary into ./build/ deb Build the installable Debian package into ./build/ clean Remove the ./build/ directory (like make clean ) docs Preview the documentation locally with live reload docs-build Render the static documentation site into ./site/ Options ¶ Option Applies to Effect -v , --verbose build Configure with -DVERBOSE_LOGGING=ON (debug build, SPDLOG_* macros active) --bash build , deb Build the TUI for a plain terminal with stock notcurses ( -DULTRAGPS_TUI_TERMINAL=bash , the default) --tmux build , deb Build the TUI for tmux, with the tmux patch applied to notcurses ( -DULTRAGPS_TUI_TERMINAL=tmux ) --no-tui build , deb Build without the notcurses terminal UI ( -DULTRAGPS_TUI=OFF ) -h , --help — Show usage Compiling the program ¶ ./build.sh build # optimised binary → ./build/UltraGpsXY ./build.sh build --verbose # debug build with verbose logging compiled in ./build.sh build --tmux # TUI build that also starts inside tmux The TUI is built in by default, in the bash variant (stock notcurses, for a plain terminal). Stock notcurses hangs at startup inside tmux 3.4 or newer, so use --tmux if you run UltraGpsXY --tui inside tmux. Run it: ./build/UltraGpsXY # or just `UltraGpsXY` if installed via the .deb Common options (see the Usage page or UltraGpsXY --help for the full list): ./build/UltraGpsXY --serial-port /dev/ttyUSB0 --baud-rate 115200 ./build/UltraGpsXY --net-device eth0 --tcp-port 9100 --udp-port 9101 --verbose Building and installing the Debian package ¶ ./build.sh deb # → ./build/ultragps-xy_<version>_amd64.deb ./build.sh deb --tmux # → ./build/ultragps-xy-tmux_<version>_amd64.deb sudo dpkg -i build/ultragps-xy_*_amd64.deb The tmux package is named ultragps-xy-tmux . It installs the same /usr/bin/UltraGpsXY and replaces ultragps-xy (only one can be installed). This installs the binary to /usr/bin/UltraGpsXY (on your PATH ) and resolves its runtime dependencies ( libc6 , libstdc++6 , libgcc-s1 ) automatically. Note The deb target builds in a temporary directory under /tmp rather than in place, then copies the finished .deb into ./build/ . This isolates the transient files dpkg-shlibdeps creates while packaging from the working tree; plain compilation is unaffected. Cleaning ¶ ./build.sh clean # removes ./build/ Terminal UI build options ¶ CMake option Default Effect ULTRAGPS_TUI ON Build the --tui interface. If the notcurses submodule or the TUI build dependencies are missing, configuring fails with a hint (use -DULTRAGPS_TUI=OFF for a headless build) ULTRAGPS_TUI_TERMINAL bash bash builds stock notcurses, for a plain terminal. tmux applies notcurses-tmux-patch-cmake/NotcursesTmuxDa1.cmake so the TUI also starts inside tmux How notcurses is built ¶ notcurses is the notcurses git submodule, pinned to the v3.0.17 commit ( 7767278 ). During the build CMake: Checks that the submodule is checked out at the commit this repository records (the gitlink). A different commit stops the configure step; run git submodule update --init notcurses to fix it. Copies the submodule into the build directory ( build/notcurses-<variant>-<commit>/src ), so the checkout itself is never modified. For the tmux variant only, runs the patch script from notcurses-tmux-patch-cmake/ on that copy. Builds notcurses-core-static and links it into UltraGpsXY . Each variant and commit gets its own copy, so switching between --bash and --tmux in the same build directory never reuses a stale tree. To move to a newer notcurses, check out the new tag in the submodule, commit the updated gitlink, and check that the patch script still finds its anchor (it fails the build if not). Why there is a tmux variant Stock notcurses (tested 3.0.9 and 3.0.17; master has the same input table) hangs inside notcurses_init() under tmux 3.4 or newer. tmux answers the Primary Device Attributes query with CSI ? 1;2;4 c , which notcurses' input automaton does not recognise. notcurses-tmux-patch-cmake/NotcursesTmuxDa1.cmake adds that reply, plus tmux's XTSMGRAPHICS error replies, to its table. A copy installed under /usr/local usually also needs a libunistring.so soname that Ubuntu 24.04 no longer ships, and no package owns it, so dpkg-shlibdeps would fail. Static linking from the submodule avoids both problems. build.sh deb refuses to package a binary that links notcurses dynamically. Previewing the documentation ¶ The docs are built with MkDocs . To preview them locally without pushing: pip install -r docs/requirements.txt # one-time: install MkDocs ./build.sh docs # live preview at http://127.0.0.1:8000 ./build.sh docs-build # render static site into ./site/ Pushing documentation changes to the release branch automatically rebuilds and republishes the site via GitHub Actions. Releasing a version ¶ Released versions live in the repository's Releases tab, each with the .deb package attached. The release branch is the stable snapshot of the most recent release. Releases are cut by pushing a version tag ( vX.Y ). Pushing the tag triggers the Release workflow, which builds the .deb and publishes a GitHub Release with it attached. To cut a release: Bump the version in CMakeLists.txt so it matches the tag you intend to push — project(UltraGpsXY VERSION X.Y ...) . The release workflow fails if the tag and the package version disagree, so this must be done first. Push that commit onto the release branch: git checkout release git merge --ff-only <your-dev-branch> git push origin release Tag the release commit and push the tag: git tag vX.Y # e.g. v1.0 — must match project(VERSION) above git push origin vX.Y The workflow then builds ultragps-xy_X.Y_amd64.deb and attaches it to a new release named "UltraGPS Ground Station vX.Y", with auto-generated notes. Users can then download and install it: sudo dpkg -i ultragps-xy_X.Y_amd64.deb

docs.text: Installation ¶ There are two ways to get UltraGpsXY onto a machine: install the prebuilt Debian package from a release, or build it from source. Install from a release (recommended) ¶ Each tagged version is published on the Releases page with two .deb packages attached: ultragps-xy_<version>_amd64.deb : the default build, for a plain terminal. ultragps-xy-tmux_<version>_amd64.deb : the tmux build. Use it if you run UltraGpsXY --tui inside tmux 3.4 or newer. It replaces ultragps-xy . Download the one you need and install it: sudo dpkg -i ultragps-xy_*_amd64.deb This installs the binary to /usr/bin/UltraGpsXY (on your PATH ) and pulls in its runtime dependencies ( libc6 , libstdc++6 , libgcc-s1 ) automatically. Prerequisites ¶ A C++17 compiler (GCC or Clang) and CMake ≥ 3.15 git (the third-party libraries are git submodules) For the terminal UI (built in by default): sudo apt install libunistring-dev libncurses-dev zlib1g-dev . notcurses comes from the notcurses submodule, so no network access is needed at build time. Without these packages configuring fails; ./build.sh build --no-tui builds without the TUI. Build from source ¶ Clone with submodules, then build with the helper script: git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/Imperious22M/UltraGPS-Ground.git cd UltraGPS-Ground # If you already cloned without --recurse-submodules: git submodule update --init --recursive ./build.sh build # optimised binary → ./build/UltraGpsXY (bash TUI) ./build.sh build --tmux # TUI that also starts inside tmux ./build.sh build --verbose # debug build with SPDLOG macros active The default bash variant uses stock notcurses. Stock notcurses hangs at startup inside tmux 3.4 or newer, so build with --tmux (which applies the patch in notcurses-tmux-patch-cmake/ ) if you run the TUI inside tmux. ./build.sh clean removes the build/ directory (equivalent to make clean ). Building without the helper script build.sh just wraps CMake: cmake -S . -B build # bash variant cmake -S . -B build -DULTRAGPS_TUI_TERMINAL=tmux # or the tmux variant cmake --build build -j "$(nproc)" Debian package (.deb) ¶ Build a .deb with the helper script: ./build.sh deb # → ./build/ultragps-xy_<version>_amd64.deb ./build.sh deb --tmux # → ./build/ultragps-xy-tmux_<version>_amd64.deb ultragps-xy-tmux installs the same /usr/bin/UltraGpsXY and replaces ultragps-xy , so only one of the two can be installed. Install it: sudo dpkg -i build/ultragps-xy_*_amd64.deb This installs the binary to /usr/bin/UltraGpsXY , so it lands on your PATH . Runtime dependencies ( libc6 , libstdc++6 , libgcc-s1 ) are resolved automatically by the package. Packaging builds in an isolated directory The deb target intentionally builds in a temporary directory under /tmp rather than in place, then copies the finished .deb into ./build/ . This isolates the transient files dpkg-shlibdeps creates while packaging from the working tree.

docs.text: There are two ways to get UltraGpsXY onto a machine: install the prebuilt Debian package from a release, or build it from source.
docs.title: Installation

docs.text: Each tagged version is published on the Releases page with two .deb packages attached: ultragps-xy_<version>_amd64.deb : the default build, for a plain terminal. ultragps-xy-tmux_<version>_amd64.deb : the tmux build. Use it if you run UltraGpsXY --tui inside tmux 3.4 or newer. It replaces ultragps-xy . Download the one you need and install it: sudo dpkg -i ultragps-xy_*_amd64.deb This installs the binary to /usr/bin/UltraGpsXY (on your PATH ) and pulls in its runtime dependencies ( libc6 , libstdc++6 , libgcc-s1 ) automatically.
docs.title: Install from a release (recommended)

docs.text: A C++17 compiler (GCC or Clang) and CMake ≥ 3.15 git (the third-party libraries are git submodules) For the terminal UI (built in by default): sudo apt install libunistring-dev libncurses-dev zlib1g-dev . notcurses comes from the notcurses submodule, so no network access is needed at build time. Without these packages configuring fails; ./build.sh build --no-tui builds without the TUI.
docs.title: Prerequisites

docs.text: Clone with submodules, then build with the helper script: git clone --recurse-submodules https://github.com/Imperious22M/UltraGPS-Ground.git cd UltraGPS-Ground # If you already cloned without --recurse-submodules: git submodule update --init --recursive ./build.sh build # optimised binary → ./build/UltraGpsXY (bash TUI) ./build.sh build --tmux # TUI that also starts inside tmux ./build.sh build --verbose # debug build with SPDLOG macros active The default bash variant uses stock notcurses. Stock notcurses hangs at startup inside tmux 3.4 or newer, so build with --tmux (which applies the patch in notcurses-tmux-patch-cmake/ ) if you run the TUI inside tmux. ./build.sh clean removes the build/ directory (equivalent to make clean ). Building without the helper script build.sh just wraps CMake: cmake -S . -B build # bash variant cmake -S . -B build -DULTRAGPS_TUI_TERMINAL=tmux # or the tmux variant cmake --build build -j "$(nproc)"
docs.title: Build from source

docs.text: Build a .deb with the helper script: ./build.sh deb # → ./build/ultragps-xy_<version>_amd64.deb ./build.sh deb --tmux # → ./build/ultragps-xy-tmux_<version>_amd64.deb ultragps-xy-tmux installs the same /usr/bin/UltraGpsXY and replaces ultragps-xy , so only one of the two can be installed. Install it: sudo dpkg -i build/ultragps-xy_*_amd64.deb This installs the binary to /usr/bin/UltraGpsXY , so it lands on your PATH . Runtime dependencies ( libc6 , libstdc++6 , libgcc-s1 ) are resolved automatically by the package. Packaging builds in an isolated directory The deb target intentionally builds in a temporary directory under /tmp rather than in place, then copies the finished .deb into ./build/ . This isolates the transient files dpkg-shlibdeps creates while packaging from the working tree.
docs.title: Debian package (.deb)

docs.text: Usage ¶ Run the program directly (if installed via the .deb , UltraGpsXY is on your PATH ; otherwise use ./build/UltraGpsXY ): UltraGpsXY [options] On startup it prints a banner summarising the resolved serial port, baud rate, IP address, and ports, then initialises the Comms module (serial link) and starts the Server module. Command-line options ¶ All configuration is done through flags — there is no configuration file read at runtime. Flag Argument Default Description -v , --verbose — off Enable verbose (debug-level) logging at runtime -s , --serial-port path /dev/ttyACM0 Serial port for the base-station Arduino -b , --baud-rate uint 38400 Baud rate; one of 9600 , 19200 , 38400 , 57600 , 115200 -n , --net-device name (auto) Network interface whose IPv4 address is shown as the server address (default: auto-detect). The server always listens on every interface -t , --tcp-port uint 9000 TCP port for the command server -u , --udp-port uint 9001 UDP port for the continuous data stream -T , --server-timeout uint (ms) 5000 Accepted for compatibility; currently unused -m , --max-clients uint 1 Maximum number of TCP clients accepted at once. Extra connections receive E: server full and are closed --no-client-limit — off Accept any number of TCP clients (the behaviour before the limit existed) --tui — off Run the interactive terminal UI (needs a TTY) --log-file path ~/.local/state/ultragps/ultragpsxy.log Where logs go while the TUI owns the terminal UltraGpsXY --help lists these options and then prints the command reference (the same text as the help command, see Command reference ). Examples ¶ Run with defaults: UltraGpsXY Custom serial port and baud rate: UltraGpsXY --serial-port /dev/ttyUSB0 --baud-rate 115200 Report a specific interface's address, use other ports, with verbose logging: UltraGpsXY --net-device eth0 --tcp-port 9100 --udp-port 9101 --verbose Runtime verbose vs. compile-time verbose --verbose raises the runtime log level to debug for direct spdlog calls. In any build this prints every message the ground station receives: TCP commands from clients, serial responses to normal commands, and serial continuous-mode data. The SPDLOG_* macros (fine-grained loop tracing) are separate and are only compiled in when the binary is built with -DVERBOSE_LOGGING=ON (see Installation ). Command reference ¶ Sending help or ? (any case) prints the reference of every command the ground station accepts: each base-station command with its syntax, what it does, its reply format and an example, plus the ground station's own behaviour. The ground station answers it itself and never sends it to the base-station, also while the base-station is booting or the serial port is closed. It works everywhere a command can be given: TCP command port: the reference comes back as text lines, to the client that asked only (other replies go to every connected client). help sent from nc . This test server was started with -t 9100 ; by default the command port is 9000. TUI: on the MAIN screen command line, or as the settings RAW COMMAND, it prints the reference into the serial link log (scrolled to its first line; PgDn reads on). The F3 HELP screen shows it too, with the TUI keys. help typed on the MAIN screen command line: the reference is printed into the SERIAL LINK log on the right. The F3 HELP screen. Command line: UltraGpsXY --help prints it after the option list. UltraGpsXY --help : the option list, then the command reference. Client limit ¶ By default only one TCP client (the control program) is accepted. The limit applies only to new connections; lowering it never drops existing sessions. UDP peers are not limited: UDP has no connection, and the control program registers with a single datagram. The limit can be changed or switched off at runtime from the TUI settings screen. Terminal UI ¶ UltraGpsXY --tui -s /dev/ttyACM0 MAIN screen (F1) Block-digit tick readout for each of the six receivers. NO ECHO means a 0 reading. Under each readout, JITTER <n> ( JIT <n> when the cell is narrow): the difference, in ticks, between the mean of that receiver's non-zero readings of the last 1 s and the mean of those of the last 10 s (exact rolling windows; 0 = no echo is left out). A higher number means the readings are moving, i.e. the transmitter is changing a lot. It is green below 5, amber below 20 and red from 20, and shows -- while either window has no reading (for example 1 s after the last reading, when not in continuous mode). One small graph per receiver (R1 to R6) of its ticks over the last 60 s. Each graph shows the per-second maximum, scales itself to that receiver's own minimum and maximum, and has the receiver's current reading in its title and the scale range in its bottom border. A red dot marks a second in which that receiver had no echo. The graphs form a grid that fits the terminal: 3 x 2 at 80x24 and 2 x 3 on larger terminals such as 160x50. The serial link log. Lines marked > were sent to the base-station, < were received from it, ! are log messages and * are TUI messages. A command line: type any base-station command (see the table below) or any raw line, then press Enter. help or ? prints the command reference into the log instead (nothing is sent). SETTINGS screen (F2 or Tab) Select an item with Up/Down (PgUp/PgDn jump 8 items, Home/End go to the first and last item), press Enter to edit it, type the value, and press Enter to apply it. Esc cancels. The list scrolls (arrows on the frame show there is more), and selecting the last item of a section also brings the status rows below it into view. The list has four sections: SERIAL LINK (HOST SIDE), NETWORK SERVER, BASE STATION (base-station commands, then its status) and TRANSMITTER STATION SETTINGS (the transmitter reset, burst delay and trigger rate, then their status). Choice items (baud rates, log level) also cycle with Left/Right. Changing the host baud rate or serial port closes and reopens the host side of the port only. The TUI then waits about 7 s for the Uno to reboot, because opening the port resets it through DTR. The host baud rate must match the rate stored in the base station (38400 by default); it is shown red when the base station has reported a different rate. BASE-STATION BAUD (B) sends B <baud> . The base station stores the rate, replies B: <baud> at the old rate and then reboots at the new rate (any valid rate reboots it, even the one in use). The ground station shows BOOTING and sends nothing for the same 7 s it waits after opening the port; only then does it switch the host side to the new rate. It switches in place on the open port: closing and reopening it would pulse DTR and reboot the Uno a second time. If the in-place switch fails, it reopens the port and waits out that boot too. Then it re-queries the settings. The rate is kept across resets. QUERY BAUD sends B 0 , which changes nothing and reports the rate in force. The same happens when a TCP client sends B , and after M when the stored rate was not 38400 (the base station then reboots back to 38400). The panel on the right shows the server IP, ports, client count and limit, and each connected TCP client and UDP peer with how long it has been connected. Commands are sent with Enter. Reset (R), delay search (D), default delay (E) and reset all settings (M) ask for confirmation first. TRANSMITTER STATION SETTINGS groups settings that are part of the base station (its commands, stored in its EEPROM) but apply to both the base station and the transmitter station. The transmitter has no serial command interface of its own; the base station passes these settings on to it: RESET (R) sends a reset packet; the transmitter reboots. DELAY SEARCH (D) and DEFAULT DELAY (E) set the burst delay, which every trigger packet carries (the transmitter waits that long after its timer match before firing). TRIGGER HZ (F) sets the trigger rate of both stations; the base station sends the new Timer1 TOP to the transmitter, which stores it in its EEPROM and reboots. M and every base-station boot send the rate too. Sync packets keep the two Timer1s phase-locked; nothing to configure. The NOTE rows at the top of that section say the same: SET ON BASE-STATION, APPLIES TO BASE + TRANSMITTER. SAMPLING MS (H) takes a value from 1 to 80 % of the trigger period (80 ms at 10 HZ) and sends H <ms> . Values outside that range are rejected in the TUI (the upper limit follows the last reported trigger rate). QUERY SAMPLING sends H 0 : the firmware changes nothing for a value out of range and replies with the sampling time still in force, so this reads the setting without changing it. TRIGGER HZ 1-50 (F) takes a rate from 1 to 50 Hz and sends F <Hz> . The base station restarts its trigger timer, tells the transmitter station (which stores the rate and resets), and sets the sampling time to its maximum, 80 % of the new period. QUERY RATE sends F 0 , which changes nothing and reports the rate, Timer1 TOP and sampling time in force. This is experimental as the system is meant to be used at a rate of 10HZ. The BASE STATION status rows show the sampling time and its Timer1 counts (16 us each, from H or F ), the stored baud rate (from B , compared with the host's) and the last reply line. The TRANSMITTER STATION SETTINGS status rows show the burst delay in force (from E or a D result), the trigger rate and Timer1 TOP (from F ), when a rate packet ( F <1..50> or M ) and a reset packet ( R ) were last sent, the last delay-search result and how many D: lines the current or last sweep has produced. ? means the base station has not reported that value yet. After M the status shows the firmware defaults (2000 us, 80 ms / 5000 counts, 10 Hz / TOP 6249). HELP screen (F3) The command reference (the same text as the help command), then the TUI keys and what the MAIN screen readouts mean. Up/Down scroll a line, PgUp/PgDn a page, Home/End go to the top and the bottom, Esc goes back to MAIN. Base-station commands (firmware base-station/src/command_control.* ). All of them except C end continuous mode. TCP clients can send the same commands. help or ? prints the full reference (see Command reference ). Command Argument Reply Effect P — N: t0, t1, t2, t3, t4, t5 One pulse; tick count per receiver, 0 = no echo S — N: t0, ..., t5 One pulse with simulated tick counts C — C: t0, ..., t5 stream Continuous mode, about 10 lines/s R — N: R Reset the transmitter station over the radio (the base station may reset itself too, if its EEPROM setting says so) D — D: <us>, <mean>, <valid>/<total> per step, then the result in the same format Burst-delay sweep, 0 to 500 us in 10 us steps by default (about 16 s); stores the winning delay E — E: <us> Store the default burst delay (2000 us) M — M: OK Reset every EEPROM setting to its default (including the 10 Hz trigger rate, re-sent to the transmitter). If the stored baud rate was not 38400, the base station reboots at 38400; the ground station waits the boot time (7 s), then switches the host side back to 38400 H <ms> integer, H 80 or H80 H: <ms>, <Timer1 counts> Set the sampling time, 1 ms to 80 % of the trigger period (at most 1000). Counts = ms x 1000 / 16 ( H: 80, 5000 ). Out of range changes nothing (a query) B <baud> integer, B 57600 or B57600 B: <stored baud> (the new rate after a change, the current one for a query) Set the base-station serial baud rate (stored in EEPROM). The reply goes out at the old rate, then the base station reboots at the new rate. The ground station waits the boot time (7 s), sending nothing, then switches the host side to the new rate in place if it supports it (9600, 19200, 38400, 57600, 115200). Rates the firmware accepts but the host cannot open (e.g. 14400, 250000) are refused by the ground station and never sent; TCP clients get ERR: B <baud> unsupported by host . An invalid rate changes nothing and does not reboot (a query, e.g. B 0 ) F <Hz> integer, F 20 or F20 F: <Hz>, <Timer1 TOP>, <sampling ms> Set the trigger rate on both stations, 1 to 50 Hz (default 10, F: 10, 6249, 80 ). TOP = round(62500 / Hz) - 1. The transmitter station stores the rate and reboots into it when the rate is new to it; the sampling time is set to its maximum, 80 % of the new period. Out of range changes nothing (a query) The firmware ignores a line it cannot decode (unknown letter, or H without a number) and sends no reply. R , D , E , F and M also act on the transmitter station over the radio. The ground station drops such lines from TCP clients. The TUI sends them anyway, so any reply shows in the log. A port or baud change that fails to open restores the previous port and baud. Keys: F1/F2/F3 switch to the MAIN, SETTINGS and HELP screens and Tab goes to the next one, PgUp/PgDn scroll the log, Up/Down recall command history, Ctrl-L redraws, and F10, Ctrl-Q or Ctrl-C quit and restore the terminal. tmux / zsh notes ¶ Inside tmux 3.4 or newer the TUI needs the tmux build ( ./build.sh build --tmux , or the ultragps-xy-tmux package). The default bash build hangs at startup there. In a plain terminal both builds work. The TUI only needs a UTF-8 terminal and a working terminfo entry ( tmux-256color , screen-256color and xterm-256color all work). The glyphs are box-drawing and block elements plus a few common single-width symbols (… · ▲ ▼ ▶ ✖), and no mouse is needed. Suggested ~/.tmux.conf : set -g default-terminal "tmux-256color" set -as terminal-features ',*:RGB' # 24-bit colour (otherwise a 256-colour approximation) set -sg escape-time 10 # tmux's 500 ms default makes Esc sluggish Pane resizes are handled live. If the terminal is ever left in a bad state (for example after a kill -9 ), run reset or stty sane .

The glyphs are box-drawing and block elements plus a few common single-width symbols (… · ▲ ▼ ▶ ✖), and no mouse is needed. Suggested ~/.tmux.conf : set -g default-terminal "tmux-256color" set -as terminal-features ',*:RGB' # 24-bit colour (otherwise a 256-colour approximation) set -sg escape-time 10 # tmux's 500 ms default makes Esc sluggish Pane resizes are handled live. If the terminal is ever left in a bad state (for example after a kill -9 ), run reset or stty sane .
